content: Estimating the number of people living with HIV is essential for planning programs and assessing resource needs. This figure serves as the denominator for key programmatic indicators and response calculations. The numerator is the estimated number of individuals infected with HIV who are alive. These estimates are generated using mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, which provide ageand gender-specific data. Spectrum AIM can also estimate the size of key populations living with HIV, though this requires data inputs that are often unavailable in many countries. National estimates for key populations living with HIV rely on modeling and data triangulation due to the challenges of sampling these populations in probability surveys that yield nationally representative results. Disaggregation of data includes gender (male, female, transgender), age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+), and key populations (men who have sex with men, people in prisons or other closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, adolescent girls, and young women). Key populations often have higher HIV prevalence than the general population in both generalized and concentrated epidemics. Stabilizing prevalence among key populations is an indicator of the success of national HIV responses. The numerator is the number of individuals in a specific key population group who test positive for HIV, while the denominator is the total number of individuals in that group tested for HIV.g., BBS) conducted every 3–5 years or annual sentinel surveillance in community or facility settings. To track changes over time, survey sites and recruitment methods should remain consistent. National-level estimates of HIV prevalence among key populations based on survey data require appropriate extrapolation methods when sufficient data are available. Disaggregation for this indicator includes key populations (men who have sex with men, people in prisons or closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals), gender (male, female, transgender), age (<25, 25+), and duration of engagement in key population-defining behaviors (e.g., less than or more than one year of sex work, injecting drugs, or having sex with men). The overarching global goal is to reduce new infections to fewer than 200,000 by 2030. The numerator is the estimated number of new infections during the reporting period, and the denominator is the total uninfected population (or person-years exposed). Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, are used to generate these estimates. These models incorporate data from geographical and population-specific surveys, surveillance data (e.g., case reporting, mortality, programmatic, and clinical data), and assumptions about HIV transmission. Disaggregation for this indicator includes gender (male, female, transgender), age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+), and key populations (men who have sex with men, people in prisons or closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals, adolescent girls, and young women). This includes providing antiretroviral therapy (ART) to pregnant and breastfeeding women living with HIV and retaining them on ART throughout pregnancy and breastfeeding to reduce transmission. The percentage of children living with HIV should decrease as coverage of prevention interventions and the use of effective ART increase. Countries have improved access to ART and strengthened counseling on infant feeding for HIV-positive pregnant and breastfeeding women. The numerator is the estimated number of children newly infected with HIV via mother-to-child transmission among women living with HIV who delivered in the past 12 months. The denominator is the estimated number of women living with HIV who delivered in the past 12 months. Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, are used to calculate the final mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) rate. These calculations require data on the number of women living with HIV giving birth (by age group), timing of ART initiation (before conception, early in pregnancy, or late in pregnancy), retention on ART at delivery, HIV incidence among pregnant and breastfeeding women, ART coverage postpartum, breastfeeding cessation rates (by child age in months), dropout rates among breastfeeding women on ART, and probabilities of MTCT based on ART regimens and infant feeding practices. In the era of the Treat All approach, effective diagnosis and treatment of people living with HIV should significantly reduce AIDS-related deaths. The numerator is the estimated number of people dying from AIDS-related causes during the calendar year, and the denominator is the total population, regardless of HIV status. Mathematical modeling tools, such as Spectrum AIM, are used to generate these estimates. These tools require demographic data, HIV prevalence, the number of people receiving ART, HIV incidence, and assumptions about survival rates. Additional data from verbal autopsy or vital reporting systems (including estimates of underreporting and misclassification) may also be used. Disaggregation for this indicator includes gender (male, female, transgender), age groups (0–4, 5–9, 10–14, 15–19, 20–24, 25–49, 50+), and key populations (men who have sex with men, people in prisons or closed settings, people who inject drugs, sex workers, transgender individuals).
